---
title: "Communicating analysis"
description: "Writing a quality assurance statement, and making sure caveats travel with the numbers."
---

Analysis that is understood wrongly is worse than analysis nobody reads, because it gets acted on.
This section covers how to communicate results so they are used for what they can support and not
for what they cannot.

*Phase 4, delivery and sign-off. [Where this sits in the lifecycle](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd).*

## What you must communicate

Analysis should be presented in a way suitable for the intended audience, with **findings, and the
limitations and uncertainty around them, communicated clearly, objectively and impartially**.[^src-govs-010-section-6-4]

GovS 010 section 5.5 says delivered results **should** include an assurance statement covering
assumptions, uncertainty, limitations, and comments on the applicability and use of the results,
together with links to references, code and data.

**At NHSBSA it is not a courtesy.** The statement is what makes an assurance level visible to
somebody who was not in the room, so this playbook requires one at every level. The standard sets the
floor and NHSBSA stands above it.

## Caveats travel with the number, or they do not travel

::: {.callout-important title="The annex rule" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
State a material caveat in the same place as the figure it qualifies. Not in an annex, not in a
methodology note, not in a footnote on a later page.

Figures get copied into slides, board papers and emails. Annexes do not follow them.

**If a caveat is too long to sit alongside the number, the number is not ready to be quoted.**
:::

This is the single most common way good analysis causes harm. The analysis is right, the caveat is
documented, and the two become separated somewhere between the report and the decision.

## The quality assurance statement

A quality assurance statement tells a reader what was done to make the analysis trustworthy, and
what its limits are. Whether you need one depends on your assurance level:

| Level | Statement |
|---|---|
| Level 1 Standard | Optional. State your main limitation alongside the result |
| Level 2 Enhanced | Required |
| Level 3 Comprehensive | Required, and **published with the output** |
| Level 4 BCA | Required, published with the output, and covered by the QA appraisal sign-off |

### A worked example

This is a Level 2 Enhanced statement. Bracketed prompts show what belongs in each place.

> This analysis was produced by [analyst], [team], NHS Business Services Authority, in [month year]
> to support [the decision it informs].
>
> It was assessed as Level 2 Enhanced on the NHSBSA assurance level decision sheet,
> on the basis that it informs a directorate-level operational decision using linked internal data
> and an established statistical method.
>
> Inputs were drawn from [source] as at [extract date]. [Named data quality issue] is present in the
> source and affects [which part of the result] by [scale or direction]. The method was independently
> reviewed by [reviewer] on [date], and the code is peer reviewed and version controlled at
> [repository].
>
> Key assumptions and their sensitivity are recorded in the project record at [link]. The principal
> limitation is [limitation], which means these results should not be used to [the specific misuse
> this analysis cannot support].
>
> Residual uncertainty is [description]. Questions about interpretation should go to [contact].

::: {.callout-note title="Why the brackets are left in" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
The failure mode of a worked example is that people copy it whole, including reasoning that does not
apply to their work. A statement claiming independent review that did not happen is worse than no
statement at all.

Bracketed prompts force a decision at each point. Fill them in or delete the sentence.
:::

### What a Level 3 statement adds

Everything above, plus:

- the Business Critical register reference
- the assurer, named, independent of the delivering team, with dates
- confirmation that code was assured against the code assurance playbook
- uncertainty quantified as a range, with its principal source
- the sensitivity testing result for the key assumption
- an Algorithm Transparency Recording Standard entry reference, where applicable
- the approver, and the next review date

## Writing well

**Lead with the finding, not the method.** The reader wants to know what you found. How you found it
matters, and it comes second.

**Say what the analysis cannot support.** The sentence "this analysis should not be used to..." does
more work than any other in a limitations section.

**Use plain language.** Plain does not mean imprecise. It means the precision is in the content
rather than the vocabulary.

**Show uncertainty in the visualisation**, not only in the text.
See [section 7](../07-uncertainty/index.qmd).

**Do not let confidence in the method become confidence in the conclusion.** A well-executed analysis
of limited data is still an analysis of limited data.

## Approval and release

The commissioner must be able to trust the results, understand any uncertainty, and have enough
assurance from the critical friend. They approve the results for release, ensure release is
appropriate and timely, and ensure the results are clear, accessible and transparent with appropriate
caveats and constraints.

Where results are published on internal or external web pages, NHSBSA accessibility guidelines apply.

**Official statistics** must follow the Code of Practice for Statistics, and the Lead Official for
Statistics or an appointed deputy must approve all official statistics outputs. Standards 7, 9 and 10
are the ones this section serves: be open about quality, be clear, be accessible.
See [section 2](../02-standards-landscape/index.qmd).

Published or unpublished management information should follow the same best practice principles.

**Presentation is part of communication.** Charts, tables and dashboards follow the
[NHSBSA Data Visualisation Standards](https://nhsbsa.github.io/nhsbsa-digital-playbook/data/data-visualisation/),
which cover how to choose a chart, how to label it and how to make it readable. Where an output
contains small counts, the **NHSBSA Statistical Disclosure Control protocol** sets the thresholds
and the methods. It is listed in
[section 12](../12-tools-and-templates/index.qmd).

## When something turns out to be wrong

Nothing in this playbook prevents an error reaching publication. What decides whether that error
damages trust is what happens next, and for official statistics NHSBSA has already written down
what happens next.

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-corrections.qmd >}}

The **NHSBSA Revisions and Corrections Policy** distinguishes a revision from a correction. A
revision is expected: statistics published as provisional and later finalised, a change of
methodology, or the arrival of further data. A correction is an error.

The policy grades errors by consequence rather than by size:

| The error | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Significant**, where the change would contradict the conclusions previously drawn from the data | A prominent alert on the website, corrected as soon as possible, and communicated to users and stakeholders |
| **Minor but significant**, insubstantial but warranting immediate correction in professional judgement | The published release is amended and the revision is clearly identified in it |
| **Minor and insignificant**, where a correction would reasonably be deemed inconsequential | Corrected at the next scheduled release rather than immediately |

Decisions on how to address an error in published statistics are made by the **Lead Official for
Statistics**, in consultation with the National Statistician as appropriate, and the amendment is
published alongside the link to the document. Where an error is known but corrected figures are not
yet available, a note goes on the statistics saying so and making clear the figures are subject to
change.[^src-nhsbsa-revisions-and-corrections-policy-v002-sections-2-and-3]

::: {.callout-note title="If your output is not official statistics" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
The policy binds official and national statistics. The behaviour it describes is worth following
anywhere: say what was wrong, say what it changed, say where the corrected version is, and leave
the original visible rather than replacing it silently.

An analysis that quietly acquires new numbers is indistinguishable from an analysis nobody checked.
:::

### Where NHSBSA analysis is published

| Output | Published at |
|---|---|
| Official statistics | [NHSBSA statistical collections](https://www.nhsbsa.nhs.uk/statistical-collections) |
| Research and insight articles | [NHSBSA data science projects](https://www.nhsbsa.nhs.uk/data-science-projects) |
| Open datasets | [NHSBSA Open Data Portal](https://opendata.nhsbsa.net/) |
| Analytical code | [NHSBSA data and analytics code repositories](https://www.nhsbsa.nhs.uk/data-and-analytics-code-repositories) |

All documentation should be stored centrally.
